title: Chapter 12 — Biographical
paragraphs: Queequeg was a native of Rokovoko, an island far away to the west and south. It isn't on any map; true places never are.

When he was a new-hatched savage running wild about his native woodlands in a grass loincloth, followed by the nibbling goats as if he were a green sapling — even then, a strong desire lurked in Queequeg's ambitious soul to see something more of Christendom than a sample whaler or two. His father was a High Chief, a King; his uncle a High Priest; and on his mother's side he boasted aunts who were the wives of unconquerable warriors. There was excellent blood in his veins — royal stuff; though sadly spoiled, I fear, by the cannibal appetite he nourished in his untutored youth.

A Sag Harbor ship visited his father's bay, and Queequeg asked for a passage to Christian lands. But the ship, having her full complement of seamen, rejected his request; and not all the influence of the King his father could prevail. But Queequeg vowed a vow. Alone in his canoe, he paddled off to a distant strait which he knew the ship must pass through when she left the island. On one side was a coral reef; on the other a low tongue of land, covered with mangrove thickets that grew out into the water. Hiding his canoe, still afloat, among these thickets, with its prow toward the sea, he sat down in the stern, paddle held low in his hand; and when the ship was gliding by, he darted out like a flash; reached her side; capsized and sank his canoe with one backward kick of his foot; climbed up the chains; and throwing himself full length on the deck, grabbed a ring-bolt there, and swore not to let go of it even if he were hacked to pieces.

In vain the captain threatened to throw him overboard and held a cutlass over his naked wrists; Queequeg was the son of a King, and Queequeg did not budge. Struck by his desperate daring, and his wild desire to visit Christendom, the captain at last relented, and told him he might make himself at home. But this fine young savage — this sea Prince of Wales — never saw the Captain's cabin. They put him down among the sailors, and made a whaleman of him. But like Czar Peter, content to toil in the shipyards of foreign cities, Queequeg scorned no apparent humiliation, if by it he might gain the power of enlightening his untutored countrymen. For at bottom — so he told me — he was moved by a profound desire to learn from the Christians the arts by which to make his people still happier than they were; and more than that, still better than they were. But alas! The practices of whalemen soon convinced him that even Christians could be both miserable and wicked — infinitely more so than all his father's heathens. Arriving at last in old Sag Harbor, and seeing what the sailors did there, and then going on to Nantucket and seeing how they spent their wages in that place too, poor Queequeg gave it up for lost. It's a wicked world in every meridian, he thought; I'll die a pagan.

So, though still an old idolater at heart, he lived among these Christians, wore their clothes, and tried to speak their gibberish. That explains his odd ways, even though he had been away from home for some time now.

Through hints, I asked him whether he did not intend to go back and have a coronation, since he might now consider his father dead and gone, as he had been very old and feeble at last report. He answered no, not yet; and added that he was afraid Christianity, or rather Christians, had made him unfit to ascend the pure and undefiled throne of thirty pagan Kings before him. But by and by, he said, he would return — as soon as he felt himself baptized again. For the time being, however, he intended to sail about and sow his wild oats in all four oceans. They had made a harpooner of him, and that barbed iron now served him in place of a scepter.

I asked him what his immediate plans might be. He answered: to go to sea again, in his old calling. At this, I told him that whaling was my own design, and told him of my intention to sail out of Nantucket, as the most promising port for an adventurous whaleman to embark from. He at once resolved to go with me to that island, ship aboard the same vessel, get into the same watch, the same boat, the same mess as me — in short, to share my every fortune, and with both my hands in his, boldly dip into the potluck of both worlds. To all this I joyfully agreed; for besides the affection I now felt for Queequeg, he was an experienced harpooner, and as such could not fail to be very useful to someone who, like me, was wholly ignorant of the mysteries of whaling, though well acquainted with the sea as merchant seamen know it.

His story finished with his pipe's last dying puff. Queequeg embraced me, pressed his forehead against mine, and blowing out the light, we rolled away from each other, this way and that, and were soon asleep.
